"'''Informer'''" is a song by Canadian [[reggae]] musician [[Snow (musician)|Snow]], released in August 1992 by [[East West Records|EastWest America]] and Motor Jam Records as the first single from his debut album, ''[[12 Inches of Snow]]'' (1993). The song is well known for the line "''a licky boom boom down''"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://genius.com/a/snows-informer-how-a-stop-snitching-anthem-became-a-no-1-pop-hit|title=Snow's "Informer": How A Stop Snitching Anthem Became A No. 1 Pop Hit|work=Genius|access-date=February 14, 2021|archive-date=February 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210203232905/https://genius.com/a/snows-informer-how-a-stop-snitching-anthem-became-a-no-1-pop-hit|url-status=live}}</ref> and for Snow's fast [[Toasting (Jamaican music)|toasting]] and often unintelligible lyrics.

Produced by [[MC Shan]], who also contributed a rap verse, "Informer" was a chart-topping hit, spending seven consecutive weeks at number one on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and reaching number one in 11 other countries. "Informer" is Snow's biggest hit in the United Kingdom, where it peaked at number two on the [[UK Singles Chart]]. Its music video was directed by George Seminara, featuring Snow in jail. In 2007, "Informer" was ranked number 84 on [[VH1]]'s "100 Greatest Songs of the 90s". Conversely, the song was included in [[Pitchfork Media|''Pitchfork'']]{{'}}s 2010 list of "The Seven Worst U.S. Number One Singles of the 90s".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pitchfork.com/features/staff-lists/7856-a-feature-about-nothing-the-1990s-in-lists/2/|title=Staff Lists|work=Pitchfork|date=September 7, 2010|access-date=December 29, 2015|archive-date=December 27, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151227061709/http://pitchfork.com/features/staff-lists/7856-a-feature-about-nothing-the-1990s-in-lists/2/|url-status=live}}</ref> 

In 2019, Puerto Rican singer, songwriter, and rapper [[Daddy Yankee]] released a new version of "Informer" as "[[Con Calma]]" together with Snow, who recorded new parts. The Spanish-language remake topped the charts of 20 countries and reached the top 10 of 10 others.

"Informer" is a song by Canadian reggae musician Snow, released in August 1992 by EastWest America and Motor Jam Records as the first single from his debut album, 12 Inches of Snow (1993). The song is well known for the line "a licky boom boom down" and for Snow's fast toasting and often unintelligible lyrics.

Produced by MC Shan, who also contributed a rap verse, "Informer" was a chart-topping hit, spending seven consecutive weeks at number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 and reaching number one in 11 other countries. "Informer" is Snow's biggest hit in the United Kingdom, where it peaked at number two on the UK Singles Chart. Its music video was directed by George Seminara, featuring Snow in jail. In 2007, "Informer" was ranked number 84 on VH1's "100 Greatest Songs of the 90s". Conversely, the song was included in Pitchfork{{'}}s 2010 list of "The Seven Worst U.S. Number One Singles of the 90s". 

In 2019, Puerto Rican singer, songwriter, and rapper Daddy Yankee released a new version of "Informer" as "Con Calma" together with Snow, who recorded new parts. The Spanish-language remake topped the charts of 20 countries and reached the top 10 of 10 others.

sections.heading: Background and content
sections.wikitext:
Snow grew up as Darrin O'Brien in [[Toronto]], Canada. He was raised on classic rock, but after Jamaicans moved into his neighborhood, due to then-Prime Minister [[Pierre Trudeau]]'s revised immigration policies, reggae became a huge part of his life.<ref name="Browne" />
{{Quote box|width=25%|align=right|quote="That's a jail song. It's not, 'Baby, I love you.' I wrote that song in jail about informers. But people didn't know what I was singing."|source=—[[Snow (musician)|Snow]] talking about the song.<ref name="Browne">{{cite magazine|last=Browne|first=David|title=Winter Is Here: Inside the Return of 'Informer' Rapper Snow|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/snow-interview-2019-informer-con-calma-837818/|magazine=Rolling Stone|date=May 21, 2019|access-date=March 4, 2020|archive-date=March 7, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200307175135/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/snow-interview-2019-informer-con-calma-837818/|url-status=live}}</ref>}}
In 1992, while on vacation in [[Queens|Queens, New York]], Snow met American rapper and record producer [[MC Shan]], and they produced a four-song demo.<ref name=Billboard1999>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|date=May 22, 1999|pages=49, 52|title=Snow Looks For Warmer Reception|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ig0EAAAAMBAJ&q=snow%20informer%20released%201992&pg=PA49 |last=LeBlanc|first=Larry}}</ref> MC Shan then introduced Snow to producer–managers Steve Salem and David Eng, who signed him to their Motor Jam Records company, and licensed the music to [[East West Records]].<ref name=Billboard1999/> Shortly thereafter, Snow began serving an eight-month sentence in Toronto for assault.<ref name=Billboard1999/> "Informer" began getting radio and [[Much (TV channel)|MuchMusic]] airplay while he was incarcerated.<ref name=Billboard1999/>

The song is based on a separate 1989 incident when Snow was charged with two counts of attempted murder.<ref name=Billboard1999/> At the time, he was detained for a year in [[Toronto]] before the charges were reduced to aggravated assault, and he was eventually acquitted and freed.<ref name=Billboard1999/> In a 1999 interview, he referred to his criminal history as "a couple of bar fights."<ref name=Billboard1999/>
sections.text:
Snow grew up as Darrin O'Brien in Toronto, Canada. He was raised on classic rock, but after Jamaicans moved into his neighborhood, due to then-Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau's revised immigration policies, reggae became a huge part of his life.
{{Quote box|width=25%|align=right|quote="That's a jail song. It's not, 'Baby, I love you.' I wrote that song in jail about informers. But people didn't know what I was singing."|source=—Snow talking about the song.}}
In 1992, while on vacation in Queens, New York, Snow met American rapper and record producer MC Shan, and they produced a four-song demo. MC Shan then introduced Snow to producer–managers Steve Salem and David Eng, who signed him to their Motor Jam Records company, and licensed the music to East West Records. Shortly thereafter, Snow began serving an eight-month sentence in Toronto for assault. "Informer" began getting radio and MuchMusic airplay while he was incarcerated.

The song is based on a separate 1989 incident when Snow was charged with two counts of attempted murder. At the time, he was detained for a year in Toronto before the charges were reduced to aggravated assault, and he was eventually acquitted and freed. In a 1999 interview, he referred to his criminal history as "a couple of bar fights."

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
[[AllMusic]] editor Ron Wynn called the song "patois-laced", noting further that it "shattered the myth that [[pop music|pop]] audiences wouldn't embrace any tune whose lyrics weren't in pristine English; when his video was released, it included a rolling translation at the bottom."<ref>{{cite web|first=Ron|last=Wynn|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/12-inches-of-snow-mw0000094642|title=Snow - 12 Inches of Snow|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=February 18, 2020|archive-date=April 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430143543/https://www.allmusic.com/album/12-inches-of-snow-mw0000094642|url-status=live}}</ref> M.R. Martinez from ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' felt it demonstrated [[Snow (musician)|Snow]]'s "unique delivery which sounds less imitative than some [[dancehall]]ers or rappers from the bonafide hood."<ref>{{cite magazine |first= M.R. |last= Martinez |title= Rap/Dance Music |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]] |date= January 23, 1993 |page= 11 |access-date= November 1, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1993/CB-1993-01-23.pdf |archive-date= August 17, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200817234550/https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1993/CB-1993-01-23.pdf |url-status= live }}</ref> [[Havelock Nelson]] from ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' declared the song as "slippery and tuneful".<ref>{{cite magazine |first= Havelock |last= Nelson |title= 12 Inches of Snow |magazine= [[Entertainment Weekly]] |date= February 26, 1993 |access-date= November 11, 2020 |url= https://ew.com/article/1993/02/26/12-inches-snow/ |author-link= Havelock Nelson |archive-date= November 18, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201118061927/https://ew.com/article/1993/02/26/12-inches-snow/ |url-status= dead }}</ref> Swedish ''[[Expressen]]'' described it as "hard-boiled [[Jamaica]]n crime fiction".<ref>''[[Expressen]]''. April 15, 1993.</ref> Katrine Ring from Danish ''[[Gaffa (magazine)|Gaffa]]'' named it an "excellent pop-number".<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://gaffa.e-pages.pub/titles/gaffa/9520/publications/124/pages/18|first=Katrine|last=Ring|title=Groove|magazine=[[Gaffa (magazine)|Gaffa]]|date=June 1, 1993|page=19|access-date=March 29, 2020|language=da|archive-date=March 29, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329070625/https://gaffa.e-pages.pub/titles/gaffa/9520/publications/124/pages/18/|url-status=live}}</ref> Dennis Hunt from ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' felt "he adds a nifty dimension to dancehall by smoothly integrating pop textures."<ref>{{cite news|first=Dennis|last=Hunt|title=In Brief|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=February 28, 1993|page=|accessdate=January 22, 2023|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-02-28-ca-54-story.html|archive-date=January 22, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230122011535/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-02-28-ca-54-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In his weekly UK chart commentary, [[James Masterton]] concluded that it "must surely be a contender for No.1 within a week or two."<ref>{{cite web|last=Masterton|first=James|title=Week Ending March 20th 1993|url=https://chart-watch.uk/archives/1993/week-ending-march-20th-1993|website=Chart Watch UK|date=March 14, 1993|accessdate=September 10, 2021|author-link=James Masterton|archive-date=February 13, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220213095218/https://chart-watch.uk/archives/1993/week-ending-march-20th-1993|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Alan Jones from ''[[Music Week]]'' complimented "this infectious, instantly appealing dancehall" song for achieving "the right mix between [[reggae]] and [[hip-hop]]." He added that it "should make quite a splash here."<ref>{{cite magazine |first= Alan |last= Jones |title= Market Preview: Mainstream - Singles |magazine= [[Music Week]] |date= March 6, 1993 |page= 19 |accessdate= March 24, 2021 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1993/Music-Week-1993-03-06.pdf |archive-date= April 14, 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220414022200/https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1993/Music-Week-1993-03-06.pdf |url-status= live }}</ref> Cermak and Ross from ''The Network Forty'' commented, "You'd swear you were listening to a Jamaican straight out of [[Kingston, Jamaica|Kingston]], but this 22-year-old white male hails from [[Toronto]]'s ghetto. Along with mixer DJ Prince and record producer and rapper [[MC Shan]], Snow creates a hooky low-groover with infectious dancehall [[Toasting (Jamaican music)|toasting]]."<ref>{{cite magazine|first1=Wendi|last1=Cermak|first2=Randy|last2=Ross|url=http://www.americanradiohistory.com/Archive-Network-40/92/Network-40-1992-11-27.pdf|title=Hot Crossover: Music Meeting|magazine=The Network Forty|date=November 27, 1992|page=45|access-date=February 21, 2018}}</ref> Jan DeKnock from ''[[Orlando Sentinel]]'' labeled it as "dancable".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1993/04/23/informer-still-champ-chart-action-stays-slow/|title='Informer' Still Champ - sections.text:
AllMusic editor Ron Wynn called the song "patois-laced", noting further that it "shattered the myth that pop audiences wouldn't embrace any tune whose lyrics weren't in pristine English; when his video was released, it included a rolling translation at the bottom." M.R. Martinez from Cash Box felt it demonstrated Snow's "unique delivery which sounds less imitative than some dancehallers or rappers from the bonafide hood." Havelock Nelson from Entertainment Weekly declared the song as "slippery and tuneful". Swedish Expressen described it as "hard-boiled Jamaican crime fiction". Katrine Ring from Danish Gaffa named it an "excellent pop-number". Dennis Hunt from Los Angeles Times felt "he adds a nifty dimension to dancehall by smoothly integrating pop textures." In his weekly UK chart commentary, James Masterton concluded that it "must surely be a contender for No.1 within a week or two." 

Alan Jones from Music Week complimented "this infectious, instantly appealing dancehall" song for achieving "the right mix between reggae and hip-hop." He added that it "should make quite a splash here." Cermak and Ross from The Network Forty commented, "You'd swear you were listening to a Jamaican straight out of Kingston, but this 22-year-old white male hails from Toronto's ghetto. Along with mixer DJ Prince and record producer and rapper MC Shan, Snow creates a hooky low-groover with infectious dancehall toasting." Jan DeKnock from Orlando Sentinel labeled it as "dancable". People Magazine noted that Snow's "incarcerations flavor the pumped up, hip-hop-infused single". James Hamilton from the Record Mirror Dance Update called it both "excellent" and "jaunty" in his weekly dance column. Parry Gettelman from The Sentinel named "Informer" one of two "best tracks" of the album, remarking that it "pair powerful rhythms with killer choruses - hear "Informer" once and just try to get it out of your head."

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext:
"Informer" peaked at number one on the singles chart in Denmark, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Mexico, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, as well as on the [[Eurochart Hot 100]]. It entered the top 10 in Austria, France, Greece, Iceland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom. In the latter country, the single peaked at number two during its third week at the [[UK Singles Chart]], on March 21, 1993.<ref name="uk"/> Outside Europe, it reached number one in Australia, New Zealand, Zimbabwe, and on the US ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Hot 100]]. In Snow's native Canada, "Informer" topped ''[[The Record (magazine)|The Record]]''{{'}}s singles chart and was a top-10 radio hit, peaking at number nine on the ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' 100 Hit Tracks chart. In West Asia, the song became a top-five hit in Israel, peaking at number two on April 13, 1993.<ref name="israel">{{cite web|url=https://israelcharts.com/|title=Israeli Charts|date=April 13, 1993|access-date=August 19, 2026|archive-date=June 26, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260626205604/https://israelcharts.com/|url-status=live}} Search "Informer" for Israeli chart history.</ref>

"Informer" was awarded with a [[Music recording certification|gold record]] in Austria and the Netherlands, a [[Music recording certification|silver record]] in the UK, and a [[Music recording certification|platinum record]] in Germany, New Zealand and the US. In Australia, it received a [[Music recording certification|double-platinum record]].

"Informer" peaked at number one on the singles chart in Denmark, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Mexico, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, as well as on the Eurochart Hot 100. It entered the top 10 in Austria, France, Greece, Iceland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom. In the latter country, the single peaked at number two during its third week at the UK Singles Chart, on March 21, 1993. Outside Europe, it reached number one in Australia, New Zealand, Zimbabwe, and on the US Billboard Hot 100. In Snow's native Canada, "Informer" topped The Record{{'}}s singles chart and was a top-10 radio hit, peaking at number nine on the RPM 100 Hit Tracks chart. In West Asia, the song became a top-five hit in Israel, peaking at number two on April 13, 1993.

"Informer" was awarded with a gold record in Austria and the Netherlands, a silver record in the UK, and a platinum record in Germany, New Zealand and the US. In Australia, it received a double-platinum record.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: Directed by George Seminara, the accompanying music video for the song shows Snow entering a jail cell. His producer and friend, [[MC Shan]], is also featured in the video; he explains how he got into prison by not turning informer. DJ Marvin Prince is seen enjoying a sauna with a couple of women. There are bikini clad women throughout and Snow is accompanied by female dancers glossed in black and white. When first shown, the video had no subtitles, but they were added because few people could comprehend what Snow was saying.{{citation needed|date=September 2018}} Later, "Informer" was made available on [[YouTube]] in 4K remaster in 2019 and had generated more than 62 million views as of late 2025.<ref>{{cite web|title=Snow - Informer (Official Music Video) [4K Remaster]|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TSffz_bl6zo|publisher=[[YouTube]]|date=September 13, 2019|access-date=April 8, 2024|archive-date=July 21, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721054945/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TSffz_bl6zo|url-status=live}}</ref>

sections.heading: Awards and recognition
sections.wikitext: "Informer" won a [[Juno Award]] for Best Reggae Recording in 1994.<ref>Juno Awards list, {{cite web |url=http://junoawards.ca/database/artist-summary/?artist_name=snow |title=JUNO Awards |access-date=January 7, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006185654/http://junoawards.ca/database/artist-summary/?artist_name=snow |archive-date=October 6, 2011}} (Retrieved January 6, 2011).</ref> In 2007, the song was ranked number 84 on [[VH1]]'s "100 Greatest Songs of the 90s".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.vh1.com/2007-12-13/top-100-songs-of-the-90s/ |title=Latest Music News - VH1 |work=VH1 News |access-date=December 29, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120214035830/http://blog.vh1.com/2007-12-13/top-100-songs-of-the-90s |archive-date=February 14, 2012}}</ref> In 2020, [[Cleveland.com]] ranked it at number 127 on their list of the best ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Hot 100]] No. 1 song of the 1990s.<ref>{{cite web |first= Tony L. |last= Smith |title= Every No. 1 song of the 1990s ranked from worst to best |website= [[Cleveland.com]] |date= October 21, 2020 |access-date= March 5, 2021 |url= https://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/2020/10/every-no-1-song-of-the-1990s-ranked-from-worst-to-best.html |archive-date= October 27, 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20221027192441/https://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/2020/10/every-no-1-song-of-the-1990s-ranked-from-worst-to-best.html |url-status= live }}</ref>

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.wikitext: Many reggae purists viewed the song, along with the works of [[Ini Kamoze]], [[Diana King]], [[Shaggy (musician)|Shaggy]] and [[Shabba Ranks]], as another example of "watered down" commercial reggae that rose to international popularity in the 1990s.<ref>Kevin O'Brien Chang and Wayne Chen, ''Reggae Routes: The Story of Jamaican music'' (Philadelphia: Temple University Press, 1998), 6–8.</ref> The song was parodied on an episode of ''[[In Living Color]]'' where fellow Toronto native [[Jim Carrey]] portrays Snow and satirizes a white man singing reggae as well as radio stations playing a song targeted towards police officers. The song was later re-imagined into [[Daddy Yankee]]'s hit single "[[Con Calma]]", which was released in 2019.
